articles.title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
articles.snippet: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
articles.full_text:
Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
- Published
Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show.
New South Wales Police told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company.
It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions.
Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing".
The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied.
MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version.
The Dark Side of Married at First Sight
Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.
Watch on iPlayer now
Married at First Sight shows single people agreeing to "marry" total strangers after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.
The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on "honeymoons", before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.
According to industry news website TV Blackbox, external, a male cast member on the current series of MAFS Australia made a formal complaint to the police after producers allegedly shared private information about him with his on-screen bride.
A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared.
"Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."
BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.
A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."
Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.
In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.
One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.
Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".
MAFS UK review due back 'any day now'
As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.
The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.
In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.
The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.
The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show.
The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.
Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.
Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".
BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.
Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.

At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
- Published
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-RhÃ´ne region.
Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.
In the towns of MouriÃ¨s and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines âin â the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post âon X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-RhÃ´ne department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."
More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.
France's weather service, MÃ©tÃ©o-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.
The alert covers CÃ´tes-d'Armor, FinistÃ¨re, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche.
Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed.
Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops.
Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday.
Two other women were confirmed dead over â the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.

articles.title: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
articles.snippet: Some cities including Lyon and Nice have banned all protests, and the French president said only authorised demos would be allowed.
articles.full_text:
French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
- Published
Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.
Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
GÃ©rald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.
"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the RhÃ´ne prefecture said in a statement.
Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la RÃ©publique was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent NuÃ±ez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron.
The ÃlysÃ©e Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.
NuÃ±ez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

articles.title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
articles.snippet: The Swiss government told the BBC that the freed national was on her way back to Switzerland.
articles.full_text:
Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
- Published
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian â have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
The Austrian and Swiss governments have both confirmed the release of their citizens.
The Swiss government said Abbt was free and on her way back to Switzerland, while Austria said Gretzmacher had been released after "intensive diplomatic efforts".
"We are all very relieved that Eva G. is free again after more than 21 months... For many months, we worked closely, discreetly, and in a spirit of trust with our regional, European, and international partners. These joint efforts have paid off," Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said in a statement.
Kidnapping of foreigners soars in Africa's lawless Sahel region
- Published2 March
The Swiss foreign ministry said the country's federal administration officials had met Abbt in Benghazi and she had received medical care.
"She is doing well under the circumstances and is currently on her way back to Switzerland," it added.
Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis thanked those involved in Abbt's release, adding that he was "relieved that [she] is free again after more than a year and a half".
The government said it had established a task force - including the foreign affairs department, police and other agencies - after the kidnapping became known.
It added that Switzerland had maintained regular contact with Austria from the outset.
Earlier, Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Under Gaddafi, many ethnic Tuaregs from Mali and Niger were recruited to join armed groups loyal to him in Libya. After he was killed, many went home. Analysts say this has been a major factor in the spread of instability in the Sahel region.
Niger and its neighbours have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

articles.title: Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive
articles.snippet: The teacher said she could not help children because she was badly injured by the attacker.
articles.full_text:
Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive
- Published
Some readers may find this article distressing.
A 54-year-old teacher who survived a mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school said she pretended to be dead so the gunman would not shoot her again.
Becky Drury, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, said in a statement shared with US media that as she tried to shut her classroom door, the gunman shot her and she fell to the floor.
"I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again," Drury said.
The attacker - who has been identified as a 16-year-old former student at the school - killed three students and a teacher before a parent from the school fatally shot him.
In her first remarks since the 15 October shooting in Bend, Oregon, Drury said that she went to see what was happening outside the special-education classroom, and after spotting the shooter, she tried to shut the door.
The attacker still managed to shoot her, so she could not help any of the children in the classroom.
"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she said. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else."
Drury suffered serious but not life-threatening harm from the shooting, which killed five-year-old Rhoam Summer, an eight and eleven-year-old, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.
Police have said another teacher - who has not been named - attempted to disarm the gunman by throwing her mobile phone. She was not injured.
A father of two other children who had followed the suspect into the school then shot and killed the attacker, who officials named as Griffin J John II.
Reports had emerged that another teacher threw herself on top of a student to protect the child during the shooting, but Drury said she wanted to clear the record about what happened on 15 October.
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she said in her statement.
Police have not yet shared a motive for the suspect, who officials say was a special-education needs student at Silver Rail.
Drury said what happened in the classroom was "unimaginable".
"[L]ike so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy," she said.

articles.title: Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
articles.snippet: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom.
articles.full_text:
Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
- Published
Yemen's Houthi movement has said it carried out an attack on an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, which Saudi authorities said killed two people and injured eight others.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation identified those killed at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.
It did not say what type of attack occurred, but the Iran-backed Houthis said on Thursday that the airport was one of the sites they had targeted with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours.
Two more people were killed on Wednesday morning by debris from a drone that was intercepted elsewhere in Eastern Province, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybah oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze, according to the ministry.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, did not claim the attack on the oil field.
In addition to Dammam's airport, he said they had targeted the Saudi defence ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis said four drones were intercepted over Eastern Province on Wednesday night, and that another four were intercepted over the provinces of Riyadh and Medina on Thursday.
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others â the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
- Published14 hours ago
UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
- Published2 days ago
On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
- Published12 October
The Houthis also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
Houthi-run media reported on Wednesday night that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.
The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.
The fighting has also displaced more than 256,000 people.
The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
articles.snippet: The congresswoman said federal agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of a federal investigation.
articles.full_text:
Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
- Published
Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid.
"With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS NOW, external.
In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation.
The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.
More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out."
Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed.
"We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".
The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".
Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one.
She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.
The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.
Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating.
Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".
Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.
He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".
At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it".
"You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

articles.title: YouTuber arrested after popular Indian finance influencer's suicide
articles.snippet: V Harish, who ran the hugely popular Instagram account "Finance with Harish", was found dead on Tuesday.
articles.full_text:
YouTuber arrested after popular Indian finance influencer's suicide
- Published
A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.
V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.
In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria.
Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".
BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denied wrongdoing in a post on X.
The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.
Account was taken down
Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.
Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".
He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.
The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.
The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.
But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.
A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others.
A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them.
According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external.
The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.
Police complaint
Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.
Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.
This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life.
"We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.
A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case".
"[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.
Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.
In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".
He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish.
"I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity.
"I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.
If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external.

articles.title: Real Madrid’s complaint over La Liga chief’s Nazi slant sent to tribunal
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: La Liga ⁠chief ⁠Javier Tebas compared Real Madrid's communication to Nazi propaganda and now faces a tribunal in Spain.
articles.full_text:
Real Madrid’s complaint over La Liga chief’s Nazi slant sent to tribunal
La Liga chief Javier Tebas compared Real Madrid’s communication to Nazi propaganda and now faces a tribunal in Spain.
La Liga President Javier Tebas could face disciplinary action for comparing Real Madrid’s communication methods with those of Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, after Spain’s National Sports Council (CSD) asked the country’s sports tribunal on Thursday to assess whether the football executive had committed an offence.
The CSD said in a statement that it had referred the matter to the country’s Administrative Court for Sport (TAD) after Tebas made the comparison in a post on social media platform X on October 16.

The TAD must determine whether Tebas’s comments could constitute a serious offence under Spain’s 1990 Sports Law, which includes “notorious and public acts that harm sporting dignity or decorum”.
The CSD said, “It is essential to preserve the values that make sport a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play.”
Spanish giants Real Madrid called for Tebas, 64, to resign after he criticised their efforts to discredit refereeing in Spain.
Tebas had said Real Madrid’s in-house TV channel often suggested that referees attempt to prevent the club from winning.
The outspoken Spanish league chief said these tactics “recall propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels”.
Tebas later attempted to clarify that he was drawing comparisons with “those propaganda techniques” and not with the ideology of the Nazis.
The La Liga chief reiterated on Thursday with another X post that his comment had “distinguished between propaganda techniques and ideology”.
Tebas also questioned why Madrid, in “accusing the refereeing system of corruption”, did “not affect sporting dignity and decorum”.
“Does it not harm clubs, referees, and millions of fans?” wrote Tebas. “Or do those values only deserve a public defence when someone responds to such attacks?”
Real Madrid criticise referees most weeks on their television channel, and last year accused officiating in Spain of being “rigged” and “totally discredited”.

articles.title: From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.
articles.full_text:
From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.
It all began on the streets.
A student-led movement has emerged as the most serious challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader, Aleksandar Vucic, ahead of Sunday’s election.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Serbia’s president resigns to run for prime minister
- list 2 of 4Serbia’s snap election: Can Vucic outmanoeuvre the student revolt?
- list 3 of 4Serbian populist leader Vucic launches campaign for prime minister
- list 4 of 4‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
Over the past two years, many citizens, teachers, professors and other experts have joined the students, a protest group that has evolved into a political movement: “Student List–Students Win” (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeđuju).
The catalyst came after the collapse of a concrete canopy at the renovated Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024. Sixteen people were killed in the tragedy, which triggered public outrage over alleged corruption and raised questions about construction safety, the quality of renovation work, and government oversight. Students who led protests have sought a fundamental overhaul of a system they deem rotten.
‘Serbia belongs to people, not to criminals’
Kosta Golubovic, a law student at the University of Novi Sad, has been involved since day one.
“Change is clearly necessary. The state must belong to its people, not to the mafia and criminals,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The way they treat the judiciary, the catastrophic conditions at the local level, mayors resorting to violence, dying villages – along with dubious privatisations, money laundering, the erosion of every single institution, police being replaced by thugs, and an education system vanishing before our eyes… these are some of the reasons why change is needed,” said Golubovic.
Demonstrations transformed into the biggest protest movement in Serbia in years, joined by tens of thousands.
The students have not called for the overthrow of Vucic. But their persistence created one of the biggest threats to the president’s long grip on power.
Vucic became prime minister in 2014. In 2017, he was elected president, a traditionally ceremonial role that he has bolstered by maintaining influence over his SNS party.
‘Vucic is afraid of us’
Opposition parties and rights watchdogs accuse Vucic and his SNS party of bribing voters, stifling media freedom, violence against opponents, and ties with organised crime.
Vucic and his allies deny these allegations. But Serbia’s rating on Transparency International’s global corruption index has worsened gradually in recent years.
“Vucic is clearly afraid of us – it’s obvious. He knows that, for the first time in 16 years, the SNS is no longer the most popular political option in the country,” Golubovic said.
The students’ efficiency is down in part to its structure.
The old student parliament at the University of Belgrade has been replaced with plenums – daily assemblies where each group votes on its course of action. Working groups focus on strategy, donations, and security. Universities in different cities coordinate so demands remain broadly aligned.
This is why the students say they do things differently. One rule is to be leaderless, making it harder for authorities to disrupt the protests. Also, demonstrations must be peaceful, and any debris has to be cleaned up. Third, all decisions must be made democratically during hour-long plenary sessions in their university faculties.
“Even though the authorities mobilised criminal groups against the students and citizens participating in the protests, the students have remained focused on their goal: to oust a government they view as authoritarian and deeply corrupt,” said Natasa Kandic, a Serbian peace activist, sociologist, and founder of the Humanitarian Law Center (HLC) in Belgrade.
“For the first time in Serbia, they have managed to lead protests entirely without violence,” she said. “The video clips we see daily represent a new culture – one defined by irony, laughter, and the deliberate disregard for primitivism and political depravity.”
‘Serious and comprehensive plan’
State-affiliated media have maligned the students. Some Serbian authorities claimed that the group has no programme, and Vucic labelled them as “terrorists”. But their leaders, experts from different fields, claim that they have a plan.
The platform is officially titled the “Student Plan” and is divided into three sections. There are 11 points.
Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and the lead candidate and ballot holder for the Student List, explained that the platform deliberately avoids setting fixed, precise deadlines for the proposed changes. He argued that such timelines can only be determined once contributors have gained insight into the “full current state of affairs”.
“[We plan] many things – too many to list – but the goal is to change the system,” said Srdanovic in a brief call to Al Jazeera.
During debates, the establishment of a special prosecutorial police unit, a law on the origin of assets, transitional justice and the renovation of rural medical clinics are some frequent themes.
Could this be implemented in the case of a victory? Kandic is sceptical.
“The student movement doesn’t possess a transformative potential – the capacity to drive social change, break with the past, and alter a political climate where convicted war criminals are celebrated, Kosovo is treated as part of Serbia, and politicians from neighboring countries are branded as enemies,” he said.

articles.title: Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Rising costs leave US workers juggling multiple jobs as financial security becomes increasingly elusive.
articles.full_text:
Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
Rising costs leave US workers juggling multiple jobs as financial security becomes increasingly elusive.
Stacy Eichel, an empty nester in Florida, spent years balancing two jobs. One was in healthcare; the other was her own venture: a small business making custom-branded merchandise for corporate clients, such as coffee mugs and T-shirts that companies hand out at conferences and holiday parties.
For Eichel, the business was more than a paycheque. It was a side hustle for a woman who couldn’t sit still, who was always hungry for the next opportunity. It was the kind of business that thrived when companies had a little extra to spend on small branded trinkets to make an otherwise mundane corporate conference something memorable.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Bombardier looks to hire 500 new workers in US, despite Trump threat
- list 2 of 4How Canadians are bracing for the impact of Trump’s trade war
- list 3 of 4US adds just 29,000 jobs as unemployment rises before midterm elections
- list 4 of 4‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
In September 2025, Eichel lost her job in marketing for a healthcare company after a merger. Suddenly, the business she had run on the side had to shoulder more of the burden of supporting her. Yet just as she needed it to provide more, the market for her products was shrinking.
Faced with uncertainty over trade policy and tariffs, alongside the growing use of artificial intelligence across the economy, companies have been tightening their spending. Custom-branded merchandise was becoming one more expense they could do without.
“The economy is such that fewer people are buying custom-branded swag because it’s more of a luxury item. When they have extra money in the budget, that’s what they’ll use it for, but now their budgets are very tight,” Eichel, who has cut back on her expenses, told Al Jazeera.
Eichel’s experience reflects a broader strain in the US labour market, where a paycheque does not necessarily translate into financial security. The headline unemployment rate captures people actively looking for work, but it does not tell the whole story of people who are working fewer hours than they want or juggling jobs that do not provide enough income.
The Department of Labor documents this through what is called the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment and underemployment. It stands at an elevated 7.6 percent. While that’s down from 8.1 percent a year ago, having a job does not necessarily mean Americans are getting ahead financially.
The U-6 measure includes people who are working part-time because they cannot find full-time jobs, as well as those who want to work but have stopped looking for a job recently.
Wallet strains
Even people who are employed full-time are finding that their earnings do not stretch as far as they once did. An estimated 4.5 million Americans were working part-time because they could not find full-time work. Meanwhile, nine million Americans held multiple jobs, accounting for 5.5 percent of all employed workers, according to the most recent jobs report.
“Underemployment is one of the most misunderstood economic problems in America because it doesn’t always look like unemployment. It looks like a college graduate working retail despite having a degree, a former executive accepting a position paying half their previous salary, or a parent working two jobs because neither provides enough hours, benefits or income to support their family,” Tara Furiani, a workforce strategist based in Richmond, Virginia, told Al Jazeera.
Average hourly wages rose 3 percent over the past year, while consumer prices increased 3.7 percent, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the US Labor Department.
That means prices have risen faster than wages, leaving many workers with less purchasing power. Overall, prices rose 0.6 percent from the previous month, while average hourly wages increased by just 0.1 percent, adding to the financial pressure on households like Eichel’s.
Eichel has cut back on expenses and scaled down some of her usual spending, including dining out and takeout, and dropped her cable service.
“I never used to think before ordering in, and now we cook everything,” Eichel said.
With the midterm elections approaching, the cost of living is becoming a greater concern for voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that the cost of living was the most important issue for voters, leading the next-closest issue by a double-digit margin, at 47 percent compared with 22 percent for “democratic norms and values”.
A separate Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy, 40 percent to 33 percent, marking the first time in 12 years that Democrats have held an advantage on the issue.
This comes as 44 percent of Americans said they had struggled to pay for at least one basic necessity over the past year, including transportation, rent or mortgage payments, medical care and food, according to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month.
Twenty percent of respondents said they had received food from a food bank or pantry over the past year.
Joshua Teicher, a New York City-based video producer in the advertising industry, said work began drying up after the COVID-19 pandemic, with opportunities dwindling further in recent years as companies tightened their budgets. Even the slow trickle of work has nearly dried up entirely.
Teicher told Al Jazeera that his financial circumstances have changed so significantly that he is now on Medicaid, government-subsidised healthcare for people in lower-income brackets. He said he is struggling to afford prescriptions and food.
“I’m having to go into my savings. Specifically, sometimes I don’t want to get a second cup of coffee because it’s like five bucks for an espresso or something like that. It’s also been harder to eat healthy. Grocery shopping, apples are just ridiculous. I find myself walking a couple of extra blocks to a cheaper store because they have cheaper apples, those sorts of things,” Teicher said.
He told Al Jazeera that his tight budget also prevents him from affording the knee surgery he needs. Cartilage in both knees has worn down. He was able to undergo surgery on his right knee to correct the problem, but cannot afford the same procedure on his left. As a result, one leg is now slightly longer than the other.
Petrol prices are another expense weighing on consumers. The average price for a gallon of gasoline (3.78 litres) on Monday was $4.29, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices daily. By comparison, the average price was $2.98 when the US and Israel first struck Iran in late February, leading to ongoing disruptions in the global market.
Market pressures
Even for Americans who have jobs, finding a better-paying position can be difficult. Although some industries have continued to add jobs, uncertainty about economic policy has contributed to what economists call a “low-hire, low-fire” labour market.
Employers are pulling back on hiring even as layoffs remain relatively low. The latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that job openings and the number of workers quitting their jobs were largely unchanged.
“I have seen highly qualified people who have not been able to find a job for 12-18 months,” Babak Hafezi, a professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.
With fewer opportunities available, workers who already have jobs may be reluctant to leave them, even if they are unhappy or want higher pay. Those looking for work face more competition for available positions, while people who are already employed may have less leverage to negotiate better salaries. That can make it harder for workers to improve their financial situations as everyday expenses continue to rise. This is leading some people who already work full-time to add on part-time jobs.
“We have people come in all the time who are teachers looking for a part-time job, or who are in other fields asking, ‘Do you know anyone hiring part-time? I just need 15–20 hours a week to make ends meet.’ At what point does this end?” Debbie Louis, who owns a coffee shop in Brooklyn, New York, told Al Jazeera.
Although industries such as hospitality and healthcare have added jobs over the last year, Hafezi said that growth could slow or reverse over the next year. He pointed to the potential impact of the Big Beautiful tax legislation, which could reduce funding for programmes that support rural hospitals, as well as immigration policies that have discouraged international travel to the US over the past year, hitting businesses that benefit from those revenues.
At the same time, US consumers are also dealing with the reality of reduced purchasing power.
“Tariffs and economic pressures from high inflation are affecting Americans’ purchasing power. As prices increase, unit consumption decreases [they buy less as] their paycheques don’t go as far,” Hafezi said.
“This ultimately leads Americans to feel poorer and less able to consume. That is the environment that many Americans in the ‘K-shaped’ economy are in.”
In a so-called K-shaped economy, wealthier US consumers continue to prosper while lower- and middle-income households fall behind. The Conference Board’s most recent consumer confidence report found that higher-income households, often supported by investment gains and greater financial reserves, are more optimistic than those in other income brackets.
“Ahead of the midterms, policymakers and employers should be examining not simply how many Americans are working, but whether available employment provides adequate wages, sufficient hours, predictable schedules, benefits and genuine opportunities for advancement. Because a paycheque and economic security are, again, not the same thing,” Furiani, the workforce strategist, added.

Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership
On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.
“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.
This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.
The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.
On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).
On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.
Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.
‘Launching a new era’
Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.
He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.
“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” he said.
Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.
Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.
He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.
The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

articles.title: Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.
articles.full_text:
Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”, as he faces declining support in the polls before national elections next week.
His remarks came after conversations with United States President Donald Trump on Sunday and a visit to Israel by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But Netanyahu offered no indication that Washington had agreed to join another offensive against Iran, let alone a campaign to bring down Iran’s leadership.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Trump praises man who punched protester at rally in South Carolina
- list 2 of 4Southeast Asia’s toxic haze spurs calls for legal action against polluters
- list 3 of 4France reports first human Shamonda virus case, says no health risk
- list 4 of 4What is the Turkiye-Libya maritime deal, and why is the EU opposing it?
While Israel has the firepower to inflict serious damage on Iran, analysts told Al Jazeera, it lacks a clear strategy for translating military gains into the overthrow of Iran’s government. Air strikes alone are unlikely to achieve that objective, while a ground invasion would demand a far greater military commitment, they said.
A renewed offensive would also mean confronting a state that has already survived two rounds of attacks and retains the means to retaliate – both against Israel and its Gulf neighbours who are hosting US military assets. US backing, meanwhile, remains uncertain, with experts questioning Washington’s appetite for renewed fighting as it is yet to find a credible prospect of forcing Iran’s government to surrender to its demands.
Does Israel have the firepower?
Israel’s ability to attack Iran is not in doubt, experts say. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera that its offensive weapons stockpiles, and “aerial refuelling” capabilities give it a substantial advantage. “Israel could again establish air superiority and strike Iranian targets,” he said.
But while Israel can inflict serious damage, analysts are sceptical that it can accomplish regime change.
Netanyahu has portrayed Iran’s leaders as a major threat since his first term as prime minister in 1996. Addressing the US Congress that July, he said, “The most dangerous of these regimes is Iran, that has wed a cruel despotism to a fanatic militancy.”
Nearly 30 years later, US participation in the June 2025 war, and again in the campaign launched on February 28 this year, delivered the military intervention Netanyahu had long sought. The overthrow of Iran’s government, however, did not follow. Netanyahu himself acknowledged the limits of airpower in March, saying, “You can’t do it only from the air.”
“There has to be a ground component, as well,” he added, without explaining what that would involve.
Caglar Kurc, an assistant professor at Abdullah Gul University in Kayseri, Turkiye, said bombing could weaken Iran’s military but not necessarily eliminate its ability to fight back. “Airpower can degrade military capabilities but cannot fully destroy offensive capabilities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Well-hidden systems would survive.”
Overthrowing the government, Kurc said, would require a willingness to deploy troops and remain on the ground for years. Israel can also no longer assume that covert methods used in earlier attacks would prove equally effective again.
Coningham described intelligence assets as “use and burn” because deploying these methods risks exposing networks that Iranian security services will investigate and disrupt.
Israel still has “human intelligence assets on the ground”, he said, while “cyberattacks” could also form part of another campaign. But using those capabilities risks revealing and sacrificing them, making the prospect of a tangible military gain an important consideration.
Covert operations and cyberattacks, in his assessment, do not offer a clear route to overthrowing Iran’s government. Coningham was similarly sceptical that Kurdish or Baloch armed groups could provide the ground force needed to challenge the state. In March, the Trump administration was said to be actively discussing providing arms to opposition Kurdish groups, according to CNN, which cited Kurdish and US officials. But this never progressed.
“Kurdish groups lacked the military capabilities to take on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),” he said.
Iran can still retaliate
Iran also does not need to match Israel aircraft-for-aircraft to make another offensive very costly, experts say.
Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, told Al Jazeera that the “Iranians likely retain sizeable stocks of missiles,” even if damage to their targeting systems may constrain their effectiveness.
“The actual antiship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran’s southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack,” Kaushal said.
Coningham said that, for Israel, sustaining its defences would be more difficult, with previous exchanges having drawn down interceptor stocks.
Repeated attacks also impose a financial burden, as Israel will be intercepting relatively inexpensive Iranian drones with far more costly defensive weapons. Over a prolonged exchange, that imbalance could place further pressure on Israel’s interceptor supplies, while Iran retains the capacity to mass-produce more cheap weapons for a lot longer.
Would Washington join another attack?
Analysts consider this unlikely, pointing to diverging political interests between Tel Aviv and Washington, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections.
The Financial Times reported this week that an Israeli proposal for renewed strikes had failed to secure Trump’s approval, although it suggested disagreement about immediate action rather than Washington ruling out future attacks altogether.
Without Trump’s participation, Coningham said, Israel would lack US capabilities for striking deeply buried facilities. These include the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs that US B-2 bombers dropped on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities in June 2025. Designed to penetrate deeply buried targets, the weapons gave Washington an offensive capability Israel could not match on its own.
Coningham also suggested that, if Israel were to attack without US support, Iran might concentrate its retaliation on Israeli territory while avoiding US targets and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Such an approach would seek to punish Israel without drawing Washington directly into the fighting, potentially further isolating a country already widely ostracised by the international community amid its genocide in Gaza.
But analysts say the central obstacle that could ultimately prevent Israel from attacking Iran is the gap between its ability to destroy military targets and its capacity to force political change within Iran.
“You cannot change a regime unless you are prepared to deploy troops and stay in the country for some years. Israel cannot control Iran. The United States would not engage in another regime change, which could take decades,” Kurc added.
