articles.title: US Army long-range fires make a splash on the frontline with China
articles.snippet: The U.S. Army has been upgrading its missiles and rocket artillery, largely in response to China's missile arsenal.
articles.full_text:
From Balabac in the southern Philippines to Hokkaido in northern Japan, U.S. Army soldiers have stepped up their training with new long-range weapons along the first island chain, working with allies in exercises that have grown larger and more complex over the past half-decade.
Freed from Cold War-era constraints, the U.S. Army has been upgrading its existing missiles and rocket artillery and developing new, longer-range systems. Those investments are largely in response to the growing size and sophistication of China’s missile arsenal, which the U.S. military worries could deny its forces access to the Western Pacific during a conflict. The intensification of training with the Philippines and Japan reflects a shared concern about China’s military capabilities.
The emphasis on long-range fires in the first island chain is visible in the extended deployments and first-of-their-kind drills involving those weapons, especially the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System. HIMARS can conduct land-attack and maritime-strike missions using guided rockets with ranges of a few dozen miles or ballistic missiles with ranges of a few hundred miles.
U.S. Army HIMARS operated in Japan for the first time in 2021 during an exercise in Hokkaido and were first deployed to Japan’s Southwest Islands, which separate the East China Sea from the wider Pacific, in 2022 for an exercise on an island northeast of Okinawa. Since then, HIMARS has been a common feature of U.S. exercises with Japan, most recently this year’s Keen Sword, for which Army HIMARS were sent to a Japanese island that is only 150 miles east of Taiwan.
The Army’s HIMARS has a longer history in the Philippines, but in recent years, U.S. and Filipino troops have employed it in new roles, such as anti-ship strikes, and in new parts of the country. Exercises in 2024 and 2025 saw HIMARS deployed to Palawan, facing the South China Sea, and to the northern coast of Luzon, facing Taiwan.
This year’s edition of Balikatan, the two countries’ largest annual exercise, showed their ability to move HIMARS around the country by land, sea and air: In April, U.S. soldiers and airmen transported a HIMARS to Itbayat, the Philippines’ northernmost municipality and only 100 miles from Taiwan, for a dry-fire exercise. A few weeks later, an Army watercraft transported a HIMARS launcher to Balabac Island, south of Palawan, for the first time for a live-fire exercise, which showed its ability “to protect shipping going into the Sulu and Celebes Sea,” the Army said.
The ability to move forces into and across the first island chain demonstrates alliance integration and sends a message to rivals, according to Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific. “It’s really a joint success story,” Clark said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C. this month.
Clark pointed to a recent exercise for which soldiers loaded HIMARS launchers on aircraft at a base in Washington state and flew them to the Philippines, all of which was visible to adversaries. “We then join munitions from Korea that were drawn out of stocks there to the Philippines, where our adversary could see it, and then we conduct a live-fire on the backend of a HIMARS rapid-infiltration operation,” Clark added. “Being able to do that, it, one, takes a lot of skill. Second, it takes a tremendous amount of partnership with, in this case, allies to assist us.”
Clark said improving capabilities in increasingly complex exercises affects adversaries’ thinking. “To be able to conduct operational maneuver and have tremendous tactical effects that then have a strategic effect on our adversary is exactly what we were looking to gain, because what that does is it gives them pause.”
Over the past two years, the U.S. Army has introduced its Mid-Range Capability, a new ground-based missile system known as Typhon, to its training in the first island chain. Typhon can fire SM-6 missiles at air and maritime targets a few hundred miles away and Tomahawk missiles at land targets up to 1,000 miles away, bringing swathes of China and Russia into range from the Philippines and Japan.
Typhon’s first overseas deployment was in 2024 in the Philippines. It has remained there since then, and in May this year, it was test-fired for the first time, striking a target in central Luzon from nearly 400 miles away. The Army sent a Typhon to Japan for the first time in August 2025 for an exercise the following month, but the weapon lingered until November that year. It returned to Japan this summer, deploying to the southernmost of Japan’s main islands for exercises in June and September and moving to a base on Okinawa for storage in October. U.S. officials told Tokyo the deployment isn’t meant to be permanent, but it has no official end date.
The Typhon was sent to the Philippines at Manila’s request and “has maintained forward presence for now over 30 consecutive months,” Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington said in a presentation at the AUSA conference. Harrington commands the recently established 7th Infantry Division/Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, which combines the 7th Infantry Division’s ground-maneuver elements with the long-range fires and non-kinetic effects of the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force.
Typhon’s presence in the Philippines has allowed for extended in-theater training, giving soldiers more insight into issues like “How do we sustain in the environment? How do you protect those types of systems in the environment? How do you connect sensor to shooter?” Harrington said in his presentation. “To be able to do that persistently forward and persistently with our ally in the Philippines and our partners is incredibly important for us.”
While the presence of HIMARS and Typhon in new places has been widely publicized, those deployments also create opportunities for U.S. troops to do less visible work to improve communications links and enhance their command-and-control networks, ensuring that friendly forces have a common operating picture of the battlefield and can use their weapons effectively in combat.
China has watched these developments warily. Beijing regularly criticizes U.S. exercises with Japan and the Philippines as provocative and destabilizing, and it has singled out Typhon deployments for vitriol. But experts cited by Chinese state media also say China has an advantage against weapons like HIMARS when they are deployed on islands near Taiwan because the islands’ small size and terrain will hinder mobility and concealment and their remoteness will make it easier to spot and block resupply efforts.
The logistical challenge is real. U.S. war games also emphasize the difficulty of resupplying small islands near Taiwan — but Harrington said it underscores the need for US forces to disperse and adopt lower-cost, lower-signature weapons alongside expensive missiles.
“This maximizes options for the Joint Force while also enhancing the protection and survivability of our soldiers,” Harrington told Defense News at AUSA. “For example, the employment of systems such as long-range one-way-attack drones, unmanned surface vessels, and long-range launched effects may enable our division to achieve a desired effect for the Joint Force while also preserving our larger, more exquisite systems until needed for a specific purpose.”

articles.title: The Pentagon wants ketamine wafers as a battlefield medicine option
articles.snippet: The Pentagon awarded a multi-million-dollar contract to the Singapore-based iX Biopharma to develop a small, ketamine-packed wafer.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon wants ketamine wafers. And it seems to want them now.
Earlier this year, the Defense Department awarded a nearly $41 million development contract to Singapore-based iX Biopharma to develop Wafermine, a small, ketamine-packed wafer that dissolves under the tongue.
Recently, the drug’s manufacturer announced that it is pursuing an emergency authorization that could make the medication available to troops before it receives full Food and Drug Administration approval, citing a September U.S. declaration of a military emergency that justifies the emergency use of drugs deemed necessary by the Pentagon.
A federal emergency use approval declaration by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services on Sept. 3 opened the possibility of early official authorization, giving the FDA a route to use unapproved medications to treat war wounds.
According to the notice, on July 15, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth determined “a military emergency, or significant potential for a military emergency, involving a heightened risk to U.S. military forces of an attack with a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear agent or agents,” or an attack with agents that would cause life-threatening injuries.
The declaration continues: “Injuries arising from these attacks may cause those forces to experience moderate to severe acute pain and place them at risk of developing life-threatening hemodynamic instability, including shock or respiratory distress.”
Because of Hegseth’s determination, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy, Jr. declared that “circumstances exist justifying the authorization of emergency use of drugs” identified by the Pentagon.
The notice did not elaborate on the emergency circumstances or state which drugs would be identified for emergency authorization.
A Politico investigation published Tuesday found that iX Biofarma’s domestic manufacturing partner lacks the Nevada license required to operate.
iX Biofarma called the non-opioid medication the “world’s first sublingual ketamine for acute moderate to severe pain,” and said the wafer enables a different delivery mechanism, letting patients absorb the ketamine through the mucous membrane into the bloodstream.
Typically administered via injection, ketamine can alleviate pain, increase euphoria and cause dissociation and amnesia.
A 2023 study found that opioid use to alleviate battlefield injuries decreased between January 2010 and December 2019, while ketamine use increased.
The researchers found that “ketamine is generally used first for more severely injured patients and has increasingly been employed by the U.S. military as the primary analgesic for combat casualties.”
The company said it received a “sole-source” award for Wafermine development, meaning it did not solicit other vendors.
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Pentagon ignored cybersecurity flaws before data breach, Marines’ lawsuit says
articles.snippet: A pair of Marines filed a class-action lawsuit Tuesday against the Pentagon over a data breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center.
articles.full_text:
A pair of Marines filed a class-action lawsuit Tuesday against the Pentagon over a data breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center, or DMDC, arguing it allowed scammers to obtain and use their personally identifiable information, or PII.
In the complaint filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, Marine veteran Tristyn Edwards and active-duty Marine Morgan Stampfli allege that they experienced fraudulent charges on their financial accounts and an increase in spam messages because of the breach.
In September, the DMDC said it had discovered a vulnerability on July 16 in a file-sharing system that allowed unauthorized users to access unencrypted files containing personal information, including full names, Social Security numbers, birth dates and military occupations.
According to the lawsuit, the vulnerability exposed millions of files containing information on service members and people affiliated with the military for approximately nine months before it was discovered.
The lawsuit also alleges that the DMDC failed to “promptly notify” affected individuals, some of whom were informed two or three months after the breach was found.
“The exposure of Plaintiff and Class members’ PII will cause various types of misuse in the coming months and years, including but not limited to, unauthorized credit card charges, unauthorized access to email accounts, identity theft, and other fraudulent use of their Private Information,” the lawsuit says.
The lawsuit argues that the Pentagon violated federal privacy laws by failing to protect personal records and maintain compliant cybersecurity systems, despite internal warnings about issues in its systems.
The complaint cites multiple reports from the Defense Department’s Office of Inspector General describing failures by both the department and the DMDC to implement adequate cybersecurity controls.
In a report published days after the breach, the OIG said that “officials have not taken the necessary actions to demonstrate that they were operating at an effective level for 14 of the 20 [Inspector General Federal Information Security Modernization Act] core metrics.”
News of the Defense Department breach emerged alongside reports of a cyberattack targeting FBI personnel files. However, the group responsible for the FBI incident has not been linked to the Pentagon breach. The department offered affected individuals 12 months of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services.
“Had [the Defense Department] properly implemented standard cybersecurity controls — such as regular review of accounts, scanning for vulnerabilities, field encryption or tokenization of sensitive PII like SSNs, and routine monitoring of system logs for suspicious activity — the Data Breach could have been avoided,” the lawsuit says.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.title: What Is Cybersecurity? | IBM
articles.snippet: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting people, systems and data from cyberattacks by using various technologies, processes and …
articles.full_text:
Cyberattacks and cybercrime can disrupt, damage and destroy businesses, communities and lives. Security incidents can lead to identity theft, extortion and the loss of sensitive information, impacts that can significantly affect businesses and the economy. By one estimate, cybercrime will cost the world economy USD 10.5 trillion per year by 2025.3
But a more pertinent question might be: “Why is cybersecurity especially important right now?”
Today, cybercriminals are using new technologies to their advantage. For instance, businesses are embracing cloud computing for efficiency and innovation. But bad actors view this advancement as an expanding attack surface ripe for exploitation.
Bad actors are also leveraging the dark web. According to the IBM X-Force® 2025 Threat Intelligence Index, sophisticated threat actors, including nation-states, are using the anonymity of the dark web to acquire new tools and resources.
They are demonstrating never-before-seen levels of coordination, automation and prowess—elevating risk from data breaches to wide-scale disruption.
The cost of cyberattacks is also growing. According to IBM’s latest Cost of a Data Breach Report, the average cost of a data breach jumped to USD 4.99 million from USD 4.44 million in 2025, a 12% spike and the highest increase since the pandemic.

articles.title: UK’s Royal Navy has ‘serious’ anti-submarine warfare gap, committee finds
articles.snippet: The Royal Navy has a “serious anti-submarine warfare gap” that weakens the U.K.'s ability to respond to Russia’s submarine and underwater sabotage threats.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The United Kingdom’s Royal Navy has a “serious anti-submarine warfare gap” that weakens the country’s ability to respond to Russia’s submarine and underwater-sabotage threat, a parliamentary committee on defense in the High North found.
The Royal Navy currently has only five Type 23 frigates for anti-submarine warfare in service, compared with a stated requirement of eight, and analysis suggests the number of frigates equipped with a towed array sonar could remain as low as five for the next three years, the Defence Committee wrote in an inquiry report published on Thursday.
Anti-submarine warfare frigates are “critical” to helping locate Russian submarines, both in the High North as well as in British home waters, including to protect the U.K.’s ballistic missile submarines that provide the country’s nuclear deterrent when entering or leaving their base in Faslane, Scotland, according to the report.
“Although new frigates will eventually join the fleet in sufficient numbers, the current fleet readiness picture raises doubts about whether the U.K. could sustain the maritime tasks required in the High North by 2030,” the committee said.
Citing the critical role of anti-submarine operations in the High North, the committee recommended the government ensures no further Type 23 frigates equipped with towed sonar leave Navy service until they’re replaced on a one-on-one basis by the future Type 26 frigates.
The U.K. has ordered eight Type 26 frigates from BAE Systems for the anti-submarine warfare role, with the lead vessel scheduled to enter service in 2028, and Minister of State for Defence Luke Pollard said in June that the program remained on track. Norway said in August 2025 it would buy five Type 26s, with delivery to start in 2030.
Should two of the Type 26 frigates being built for the U.K. instead go to Norway to meet the delivery deadline, the Royal Navy would take until 2037 to meet its requirement for a fleet of eight frigates equipped with a towed array sonar.
“Export success must not come at the expense of the Royal Navy’s own Type 26 frigate delivery timelines,” the committee said. “The government must ensure that naval exports expand industrial capacity and allied capability, rather than competing with U.K. requirements for scarce ships, systems and skilled labor.”
The High North, which the committee defined as the greater Arctic and parts of the North Atlantic, “has become central” in U.K. defense and security concerns, with climate change increasing access to the region, according to the report.
As melting ice sheets and sea ice expose Russian bases that were previously mostly inaccessible, Russia is seeking both to defend those bases as well as project force into the Atlantic and U.K. territorial waters, according to the committee. That threatens NATO supply lines from the United States to Europe, as well as undersea and onshore infrastructure, including the U.K.’s nuclear deterrent.
Lack of a credible under-ice capability means the Navy is less able to contest Russian freedom of action in the High North, which risks forcing the U.K. into a more defensive posture, according to the report. The Defence Committee asked the government to brief panel members on progress towards re-establishing an under-ice capability for at least some of the country’s Astute-class nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The Navy’s ASW frigates and nuclear-powered submarines offer the greatest deterrent against the threat posed by Russian submarines and underwater sabotage, though “unfortunately, they are either aging or too often unavailable due to maintenance issues,” the committee report said.
For the U.K. to lead an effective coalition would require the country to address “glaring gaps” in the availability of its maritime forces, and an agreed plan with European allies to deter and if necessary defeat any aggression in the High North from 2030, according to the report.
The committee asked the Ministry of Defence to provide a classified assessment of the capability gaps in case of a conflict in the High North in 2030 in which the U.K. and allies would operate without U.S. support.
“Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements,” the report said. “With 2030 identified as a key date by which to be ready to deter or defeat any Russian threat, dramatic progress is required before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the U.K.’s Armed Forces for operations in the High North.”
The Royal Navy has a requirement for 13 frigates and six destroyers, but has struggled to meet those numbers, the committee said, with only the five Type 23 frigates and six Type 45 destroyers in service.
With the Northern Sea Route becoming more accessible, Russia may try to turn control there into a monopoly, and the government should prepare options for a U.K. state-owned vessel to transit the route to support freedom of navigation, the committee said. Sailing from Shanghai to Rotterdam takes about 14,900 kilometers via the northern route, compared with 19,500 km via the Suez Canal.
The report raised questions about the U.K.’s Hybrid Navy program to combine crewed and uncrewed vessels, saying the High North is “an exceptionally demanding environment” for autonomous systems, and the concept should not become a substitute for crewed capability before unmanned systems have been proven in harsh Arctic conditions.
The committee recommended the government explain within a year how it will test the Hybrid Navy’s main uncrewed systems in High North conditions before relying on them for operational tasks, looking at issues such as cold-weather performance, resistance to jamming and protection from capture.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

articles.title: Ukraine to be able to buy military supplies via NATO agency: report
articles.snippet: The deal comes amid worsening U.S.-Ukraine relations since U.S. President Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia this month to lower U.S. prices.
articles.full_text:
NATO will allow Ukraine to buy weapons, ammunition and military equipment via its centralized procurement agency, potentially allowing Kyiv to obtain defense supplies faster and more cheaply, the Financial Times reported on Thursday.
“It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services and access to established industrial base,” the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) director of support to operations, Jacqueline Borsboom, told the FT.
The deal comes amid worsening U.S.-Ukraine relations since U.S. President Donald Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia this month to lower U.S. fuel prices.
Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and its use of the Starshield satellite system, though Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said a meeting in Oslo on Tuesday had agreed to resolve those issues.

articles.title: US Air Force outlines the fighter fleet it needs by 2035
articles.snippet: A new Air Force report calls for 1,509 combat-coded fighters by 2035, with F-35s making up 40% of the fleet and F-47s replacing F-22s.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force says it needs 1,509 combat-coded fighters, or jets assigned to combat units, by 2035, according to a new force structure report the service sent to Congress Oct. 16.
Lt. Gen. David Tabor, the Air Force’s deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, described the report at an Oct. 20 Pentagon roundtable with reporters, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Reporters did not receive a copy of the report, and the service did not respond to a Defense News request for it by publication.
F-35s would make up about 40% of the fleet by 2035, up from about 30% today, according to figures Tabor cited. F-22s and their replacement, the F-47, would make up about 20%. The service plans to replace its F-22s with about the same number of F-47s, Tabor said.
F-15s and F-16s would split the remaining 40% about evenly. The figures exclude A-10s, which are not currently part of the Air Force’s plans for 2035.
Tabor said the analysis was based on what regional commanders say they need to carry out their missions at medium risk. The military rates risk on four levels: low, medium, significant and high. At medium risk, forces would likely achieve their goals but could be strained in long operations.
The analysis began before the war with Iran this year and was not driven by it, Tabor said. He cautioned that the 1,509 figure is likely to change with world events, new requirements and the rise of new technology.
Reaching the goal depends on Congress funding the jets and on Lockheed Martin and Boeing building them in time, Tabor said. Industry has “assured us that they can, and we believe them,” he told reporters, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Air Force officials have long said the service needs to buy 72 fighters a year. The fiscal 2027 request seeks 38 F-35s and 24 F-15EXs, a total of 62. Tabor said purchases can increase over time.
The budget counts on $2.34 billion to pay for 14 of the 38 F-35s. That money would come through a reconciliation bill, a budget package that can pass the Senate with a simple majority. If that bill fails, Tabor said, the service could pull money from other programs or push the buys to 2028.
The Air Force is seeking multiyear contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX, a request now pending in Congress. Tabor said such deals would give industry more stability to expand production.
Older F-16s reach the end of their service lives in the mid-2030s, Tabor said, but the service has not decided whether to buy a new-build F-16, tentatively called the F-16G. That decision likely won’t come in the fiscal 2028 budget, he said.
The 1,509 figure does not count Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCAs, the drone wingmen that will fly alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force plans to field 500 CCAs by 2032. Tabor said the drones are not yet changing the fighter requirement but could reduce it in future reports.
Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

articles.title: Air Force needs 1,509 combat-ready jets by 2035, service tells Congress
articles.snippet: Lt. Gen. David Tabor also confirmed reporting that the Air Force is considering a new build F-16, but said that decision wasn’t “urgent.”
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Air Force predicts it’ll need 1,509 combat-ready fighter jets by 2035 to cover a “moderate risk” operational profile, according to a senior officer and a new report reviewed by Breaking Defense.
The figure is likely a jump of dozens of aircraft from last year’s estimates, based on significant increases in a parallel “low risk” calculation.
The new figures are laid out in the congressionally mandated report dated August 2026 and sent to lawmakers as part of an unclassified update to a similar study issued last year. Along with revising fighter totals, this year’s analysis covering fiscal year 2026 makes a renewed case for changing how combat-ready fighters are counted, citing lessons from the war against Iran.
In addition to the moderate risk projection of 1,509 aircraft, in its fighter force structure report this year, the Air Force found that 1,723 combat-ready aircraft are needed to reach a low-risk operational profile by 2035 — scores more airframes than a prediction from just last year of 1,558.
The moderate risk projection is likely the most relevant one, according to Air Force Lt. Gen. David Tabor, who said officials “generally don’t plan to low risk.” Speaking to a small group of reporters at the Pentagon on Tuesday, Tabor said officials instead aim for “a moderate level of risk.”
The report’s detailed fighter projections “give[s] the public and the media and Congress confidence that we’re not making this up,” said Tabor, the Air Force’s deputy chief of staff for plans and programs.
“We are looking at the long term, and we’re setting a chart to get there, and we can’t get there on our own,” he added.
The general emphasized that exact figures in the report are somewhat “debatable” since analysis is constantly refreshed. It’s also unclear how much of an increase this year’s medium risk count of 1,509 aircraft is since the last prediction, as last year’s report did not include figures for a medium-risk operational profile.
Even as moving targets, however, the figures will likely run into the wall that is reliable congressional funding. Historically, the service has struggled to fund fighter procurement at levels it desires amid competing priorities like modernizing its nuclear arsenal and budget fights on Capitol Hill. And by rejecting certain divestments, lawmakers often require the Air Force to keep certain aircraft around longer than military officials plan, requiring them to spend more money on maintaining aging platforms.
“Without the TOA [total obligation authority], the money available, we’re not going to be able to do this,” Tabor said bluntly.
The Air Force’s FY27 budget shows some of those challenges. The Air Force included funds for 24 F-15EXs and an identical number of F-35s in its base budget, but is banking on reconciliation to provide an additional 14 F-35s. That reconciliation bill is now in doubt.
Tabor said options like shifting other money around in the base budget could be on the table if reconciliation fails to pass, but emphasized alternatives are not desirable.
“The baseline premise is we need it all,” he said.
RELATED: With reconciliation uncertain, Pentagon eyeing plan to retool FY27 priorities with Congress
Additionally, achieving a fleet of 1,509 aircraft relies on industry’s ability to deliver, which is not guaranteed. The report notes that modernization setbacks for the Lockheed Martin F-35 have driven delays, while production struggles have postponed deliveries for Boeing’s F-15EX.
Boeing said in a statement to Breaking Defense that the company “is working closely with the U.S. Air Force and Department of War to ramp up F-15EX production, including investing across the production system and expanding team training to increase production capacity.”
A Lockheed spokesperson called the F-35 “indispensable to global security” in a statement to Breaking Defense. The aircraft “has flown more than 1.2 million hours, with more than 1,375 aircraft delivered and a fleet operated by 13 nations—and growing,” the spokesperson said. “With TR-3 development completed in 2025, we’re advancing Block 4 modernization and are on pace to deliver 156 aircraft in 2026, strengthening allied and partner airpower globally.”
Tabor noted that multi-year procurement negotiations for fighter aircraft are underway. Should those longer-term agreements materialize, the general said they’d provide an important, predictive demand signal for industry.
“I personally think that yes, that is a good incentive for them to actually see the money into the future and not be beholden to this kind of erratic appropriation process” he said. “It would be great if we can get on that path.”
A New F-16?
While the F-35, F-15EX and eventually the sixth-generation F-47 will be key platforms to boost the Air Force’s fighter inventory, the service is also weighing other options including a new-build F-16.
As previously reported by multiple media outlets, Tabor confirmed that the Air Force is weighing whether to buy a new F-16 to recapitalize older aircraft. Still, he said a final decision is not “urgent” and could be made in the coming years.
“It is something that we’re talking about, and so the way I describe it is that there is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” Tabor said. “We want to be in a position that when we make this decision, that we can show our homework and be proud of it.”
In the meantime, the past year has seen a dramatic shift in the Air Force’s fighter outlook. One key change is a plan to more than double the F-15EX fleet. Another is to extend the use of a small number of A-10 squadrons out to the end of the decade. The platform has since seen combat in the Middle East under Operation Epic Fury.
Air Force platforms, like several F-15s, have been among the 81 airframes damaged or lost during the Iran conflict, according to a count by the Congressional Research Service. The new Air Force report says that despite those losses, the service still retains a total of 212 F-15Es in different versions.
Tabor asserted the fresh analysis in the report, including revised figures, was not driven by Epic Fury, reasoning that work predated the start of the conflict.
“The analysis takes some amount of time and to be fair, it should be something that we’re constantly looking at,” he said. “It really was just a refresh of the numbers and the combatant command requirements that they were articulating.”
Arithmetic Arguments
Though Tabor said the changes in aircraft figures were not driven by the conflict in Iran, some of the report’s arguments for how the fleet is counted are.
The service maintains in the report that its preferred metric of a Combat Coded Total Aircraft Inventory (CC TAI) is “fundamentally more accurate” than the Primary Mission Aircraft Inventory (PMAI) measurement preferred by Congress.
Lawmakers have set a PMAI floor of 1,145 tactical aircraft, a requirement the Air Force does not currently meet. Counting aircraft using the CC TAI method — which adds backup and attrition reserve aircraft along with the PMAI — would reflect a greater inventory, as the charts below from the report show.
The report contends that PMAI does not accurately reflect the Air Force’s true combat capacity, since backup and attrition reserve aircraft will also be called upon in wartime — as aircraft were in Epic Fury. Additionally, the report says CC TAI more accurately reflects consequences of peer conflict, since the Iran conflict showed “sustainment challenges and losses” from more intensive combat operations.
“Combat coded total aircraft inventory is a much more kind of honest look at what I think Congress and, frankly, the American people care about, which is combat capability as opposed to the primary mission aircraft inventory,” Tabor said.
Critics of the CC TAI method assert that the accounting method can leave the Air Force shortchanged since PMAI aircraft are funded at different rates than backup and attrition reserve jets, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The Air Force’s target of 1,509 jets by 2035 is measured using the CC TAI figure. Tabor said officials are still in talks with Congress about changing the metric.
“We’ve been having a lot of conversations with Congress about that language. I think that it’s a transition. It won’t be a flip of the switch that changes it, but we think we’re in a pretty good position on that,” he said.

articles.title: Pentagon AI oversight office struggles to keep pace with department’s ambitions, GAO finds
articles.snippet: The Pentagon office tapped in 2022 to oversee the military’s responsible use of AI had filled just three of 10 authorized positions as of February 2026.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon office tapped in 2022 to oversee the military’s responsible use of artificial intelligence had filled just three of its 10 authorized positions for the mission as of February 2026, even as the department pursues a strategy to accelerate AI development, a government watchdog found.
The Government Accountability Office discovered that 29 of 64 efforts outlined in the Defense Department’s Responsible AI Strategy and Implementation Pathway remained incomplete as of April 2026.
According to a report published Oct. 14, the GAO also found that staffing shortages had hindered the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer’s ability to take additional steps to implement responsible AI, which the department uses to help accelerate AI adoption.
GAO recommended that the department address staffing needs in its Responsible AI Division, which falls under the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, and issue a formal charter for the working council.
“Responsible AI should be considered the same as operationally effective AI,” said Owen Daniels, associate director of analysis at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Effective testing, evaluation, verification and validation practices can help the military manage risks while ensuring systems operate as intended and operators understand their strengths and limitations, Daniels said.
Council ‘at risk of lapsing’
The GAO found that the Responsible AI Working Council did not meet from late 2024 until August 2025.
Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer, or CDAO, officials told the watchdog agency that other priorities, including developing guidance for generative AI and contributing to government-wide AI risk-management resources, had prevented the Responsible AI Division from organizing meetings.
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., raised a related concern about accountability during a May 2025 hearing regarding the Pentagon’s AI posture.
“It’s my observation that the Defense Department doesn’t lack in the number of principals, but rather, it often struggles with too little clarity in who is responsible for what.”
Officials from four DoD components told the GAO they faced implementation challenges during the hiatus that could have benefited from greater collaboration.
Six of the 10 DoD components surveyed said sharing responsible AI resources and best practices would increase their ability to incorporate the department’s six Responsible AI tenets into their AI use cases.
The council resumed meetings in August 2025, but the GAO found it still lacked a formal charter defining its responsibilities and specifying how frequently it should meet.
“Without a charter that defines roles and responsibilities for the council ... and that specifies the frequency of council meetings, the council is at risk of lapsing again,” the GAO report reads. “Such a lapse could increase the risk of DOD facing Responsible AI implementation issues that it would not have the collaborative capacity to swiftly and effectively resolve.”
Slow staffing
CDAO officials told the GAO they were unlikely to fill vacant positions or increase staffing while the office underwent restructuring, following its realignment to the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering.
In response, the GAO argued that “by ... taking action to ensure it has staff in place to meet those needs,” CDAO could make better progress toward its goal of accelerating AI across the department.
Daniels said the staffing shortfall could make it more difficult to build AI literacy throughout the force.
“Operationally, the force needs to become AI literate, as warfighters will be responsible for determining when to deploy AI-enabled systems,” he said.
Service members need to understand AI systems’ limitations and recognize when delegating decisions to machines may be inappropriate, rather than defaulting to a machine’s judgment, Daniels said.
“Exercising meaningful human control — or to use the department’s term, appropriate levels of human judgment — over a military AI system requires robustly understanding a system’s operating boundaries through development, rigorous testing and evaluation, and training,” he said.
Congress’ role
The DoD agreed with the GAO’s two recommendations to issue a charter for the Responsible AI Working Council and address the Responsible AI Division’s workforce needs, according to the watchdog.
The GAO also urged Congress to order the department to implement earlier recommendations, including defining the responsibilities of organizations involved in AI activities and assigning responsibility and a timeline for identifying and managing the department’s AI workforce.
In a Sept. 21 letter, Sens. Jack Reed, D-R.I., Mark Warner, D-Va., and Chris Coons, D-Del., expressed concern that the Pentagon’s AI push could be outpacing its governance efforts.
“Recent events have given us growing concern about the extent to which agencies under your oversight have prioritized acceleration of AI capability adoption and ‘experimentation’ over effective governance,” the letter reads.
Reed has also called for Congress to establish clearer guardrails for military AI.
“Congress must do its job and provide balanced oversight, standards, and rules of the road,” he said.
Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

articles.title: Got milk? US Army refines its pasteurization power
articles.snippet: Thirteen U.S. Army Veterinary Corps officers milked a trip to Denmark last month, completing Europe Dairy Pasteurization Audit Training.
articles.full_text:
Thirteen U.S. Army Veterinary Corps officers milked a trip to Denmark last month, completing Europe Dairy Pasteurization Audit Training in the seaport city of Kolding.
The service said the course — which included on-site field evaluations at eight Danish dairy facilities currently approved for U.S. military procurement — aimed to ensure military members and their families overseas receive dairy that meets or exceeds U.S. standards.
In the U.S., commercial milk must be processed according to the Food and Drug Administration’s Pasteurized Milk Ordinance. Because commercial pasteurization methods are “udderly” different across the world, the course gives officers the skills to evaluate pasteurization technology in different regions, the Army said in a Monday release. The course has been taught and revised since 2004.
Military auditors from around the world, including Public Health Command Pacific, Area Support Group Kuwait and Public Multinational Force and Observers Egypt, trained to improve their pasteurization skills. Public Health Command Europe is unique, the service said, because it offers military inspectors the chance to see more than 65 pasteurizer setups.
During the course, led by Chief Warrant Officer 4 Clayton Davenport, the command food safety officer for Public Health Command Europe, the Army said officers gained realistic experience assessing equipment in operation.
“The primary training objective was to provide progressive and sequential auditor development training in pasteurizer operations that enhances understanding of the public health controls of various pasteurizers,” Davenport said in the release. “Maintaining specialized auditing capabilities remains essential to force health protection, particularly amid budgetary pressures.”
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Navy awards Applied Intuition $25M to deploy AI sensor fusion at sea
articles.snippet: The Intelligent Perception System will help sailors understand a flood of sensor feeds while collecting data to train improved AI models, the company said.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Applied Intuition has won a $25 million contract from the US Navy to begin deploying AI-powered sensor fusion on warships, starting with five Arleigh Burke-class destroyers but potentially expanding “across the fleet,” the company announced this morning.
The new Intelligent Perception System (IPS) will do two jobs at once, Applied said in its announcement and a blog post. In near real time, IPS will pull in data from various cameras and infrared sensors — many of which were never designed to work together — and synthesize a single, coherent picture for the sailors. It’ll even offer helpful features like “automated alerts” when another vessel is approaching on a collision course.
Sailors aboard the USS Fitzgerald and McCain definitely could have benefited from such a capability during their back-to-back collision incidents in 2017, which killed 17 sailors and severely damaged both ships.
Meanwhile, IPS will also record the sensor data and — when bandwidth is available and security conditions permit — transmit it back to shore. There, the system’s land-based component can analyze the collected data and use it to train improved AI models for both manned and unmanned vessels.
The system even allows ships to receive updates over the air while still at sea, instead of waiting for maintenance and modernization in port, the company said. That could enable multiple refresh cycles in a single deployment.
That kind of fast-paced adaptation is reminiscent of the drone war in Ukraine and fits with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s push for rapid upgrades. It also jibes with the Pentagon’s desire to piggyback off advances in commercial tech rather than waiting for bespoke military developments.
Applied originally focused on self-driving cars — still a major part of its business — before it branched out into defense. At its core, the technology it’s bringing to the Navy draws on that dual-use foundation.
“The amount of data the Navy collects, and the operating environments it is constantly engaged in, [are] very similar to what we do gathering data to develop driverless cars,” Jason Brown, general manager at Applied Intuition, said in a statement to Breaking Defense.
While details obviously vary, the essentials are the same for “any autonomous system that needs to perceive environments in order to feed planning and control algorithms,” he argued. “We built those data engines for our commercial business and applied the same technical approach to naval operations.”
This new contract isn’t the first time Applied has brought its technology to the Navy. IPS builds on an earlier pilot program called DECK — short for Data Edge Collection Kit— that was tested on at least one Navy vessel earlier this year.
“DECK was massively successful,” Brown declared. “It collected data, transported it — all with commercial technology — and did it securely and within Navy operational constraints.”

articles.title: Army unit experimenting with small drones for ‘tailored cyber effects’
articles.snippet: The Army is testing drone-mounted cyber and electronic warfare capabilities as it works to determine the standard-issue equipment for its 11th Cyber Battalion and a forthcoming second battalion.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — As the Army continues to determine the standard issue equipment for the 11th Cyber Battalion, it is experimenting with drones capable of delivering “tailored cyber effects” and jamming, according to an acquisition official.
The Army is testing its Radiofrequency Delivery Effects Platform (RDEP) on small drones, using a mix of government-developed and commercial-off-the-shelf payloads to deliver “non-kinetic effects” at the tactical edge, Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare, told Breaking Defense. While Bergmann didn’t specify, those are typically jamming capabilities as well as gaining access to Wi-Fi systems, to name a few.
RDEP is a hardware and software capability that allows operators to load exploits onto cards and deliver digital bullets to blind or gain access to adversary systems. The Army is exploring how the system and other payloads can support real-time spectrum monitoring and tailored cyber effects — extending the reach of tactical cyber operations while minimizing unintended impacts on friendly systems, Bergmann said during an interview at the Association of the US Army’s annual conference last week.
The efforts are part of continued experimentation to determine the right mix of equipment, capabilities and platforms for the 11th Cyber Battalion and forthcoming 12th Cyber Battalion. Bergmann assumed the brand new role of project manager in July, leading an acquisition office that combines the Army’s offensive and defensive cyber efforts.
The 11th Cyber Battalion was established in 2022, building on the Army’s earlier 915th Cyber Warfare Battalion, which dates to 2019. The unit conducts tactical-level cyber operations, primarily through radio-frequency, electronic warfare and information operations, with operators working alongside ground forces. Its Expeditionary Cyber Teams (ECTs) are scalable units that can support traditional Army formations with these non-kinetic capabilities by request.
The Army plans to establish the 12th Cyber Battalion in the coming months as a replica of the 11th, increasing the service’s capacity to conduct these operations.
The 11th Cyber Battalion does not yet have an established program of record for its standard issue equipment, and the Army is continuing to experiment with different capabilities and configurations before deciding what will enter production.
Bergmann said the Army is gathering feedback from 11th on what capabilities its drones need to support — including offensive cyber, radio-frequency and other effects.
After providing an initial prototype for teams to test, Army Cyber Command is developing a draft of the kits, he added.
“How many of these different things does the ECT need? How much of this capability does the 11th need from a cyber perspective, how much EW capability [do] they need? Where do those overlap, and what makes the best sense to outfit the ECTs that are deployed forward,” he said, describing the questions driving the effort.
The Army has leveraged existing program-of-record gear within their experiments, such as the Terrestrial Layer System Manpack, a backpack-based system that can sense and jam signals, as well as the RDEP. But the service still needs to determine which capabilities and form factors make the most sense for the 11th and its ECTs.
The Army is looking at dismounted systems, platform-based and drone-mounted payloads capable of delivering cyber and jamming effects. The service must also determine which vehicles each battalion will use, what individual ECTs will be expected to do and how much of each capability they will need.
“We’re really trying to give the commander the flexibility to have and employ which of those capabilities he or she needs,” Bergmann said.
ECTs from the 11th have been deploying on a rotating basis to support operations at the southern border over the last year, providing lessons to inform the Army’s equipment decisions. Those experiences have helped assess requirements for ground-based and man-portable capabilities, as well as the types of drones and payloads the teams need, Bergmann said.
“This next year we have not made decision on what we’re going to go into production with. We’re still doing prototypes across the various different form factors,” Bergmann said. “We have some opportunities in the next year that we’re going to get with [the 11th] to get more feedback on that.”

articles.title: How uncrewed surface vessels performing ISR help build persistent maritime awareness
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Think of sensing and detection as a network as opposed to individual unmanned surface vessels.
articles.full_text:
The intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) used to build persistent awareness of real-time activity has taken a leap forward due to the Navy’s effort to advance this capability with unmanned surface vessels (USVs). The goal is to detect, track, and interdict potential threats quickly and at standoff distances.
Building this awareness is critical to potential future naval conflicts, especially in the Indo-Pacific region. As adversaries conduct exercises and operations in gray zone maritime environments, maintaining situational awareness helps identify potential threats and decide how to respond to them, said Ben Pinx, Principal, Technology and Mission Solutions, Lyntris.
“It’s easy to see something’s moving, I have dots moving all over,” said Pinx. “Now I need to shoot at those dots or I need to create a weapon-engagement envelope to keep those adversary dots out. That’s the threat scenario that leads into what it would look like if we went to full-scale combat in the INDOPACOM area of responsibility (AOR).”
The key is building a persistent maritime awareness infrastructure that allows the Navy to sense, track and share information with other forces and allies at the speed of relevance. That will require a multi-domain, multifaceted approach to ensure coverage is in place where it is needed to paint an accurate picture of what is happening in a region.
From detection to persistent awareness
Sensing is the foundation of ISR efforts, collecting and sharing data on what is happening within a given sensor’s reach. But going beyond just data collection to understand what is actually happening in a given area creates multiple challenges. Persistent awareness requires enough coverage over time to notice changes, establish patterns, examine anomalies and maintain track continuity after the initial detection.
“It’s very easy for us to say that we’ve got coverage, we’ve got this set of satellites, or we can put P8s in areas that we want,” said Jack Zaientz, Vice President of C4I and Autonomy, Lyntris. “But each one of those has a very narrow aperture. While we can maintain coverage broadly over a large area, we can’t cover any particular spot with persistence. That is a much harder problem.
“For the Air Force that is operating in the air doing the strike, that’s OK. For the Army that is trying to do logistics or the Navy that’s trying to do prepositioning, that’s not OK. They need specific information about the areas they’re operating at a very small scale with a persistent view that is hard to achieve with airborne assets that are on the move and that are limited.”
Solving this challenge requires more assets, but it’s not as simple as adding more vessels to the fleet. Their capabilities are the critical component, and building a sense-and-detect infrastructure that can give operators and commanders the information they need to make decisions requires building awareness capabilities across multiple domains.
It also requires a mindset shift. It’s not just deploying assets, said Zaientz.
“What we want to see is that the Army and the Navy operating there stop thinking about boats as individual task assets, and instead think about the network (of USVs) as its own unit,” he said. “We are going to place a network here. Once you think about it from that command posture, you then start asking the resource question of how do I feed in new small USVs? How do I pull out? How do I manage that network? But the network stays intact, stays robust across whatever the AOR that you’ve defined.”
By thinking of sensing and detection as a network as opposed to individual assets, decision-makers can implement comprehensive strategies to gain better understanding of what is happening in an area. This is especially important in the Pacific, where vast distances make continuous local coverage difficult to sustain. While there is an extensive sensor infrastructure in place, maintaining persistent awareness across chokepoints, harbor approaches and logistics routes remains a challenge, and smaller, more agile vessels carrying ISR and communications systems can help fill in the gaps, said Pinx.
“By extending our sensing capabilities using small USVs where we’re able to go out for 190-hours plus and then loiter in certain areas, it starts taking that giant blue ocean and shrinks it down into more manageable areas of interest so that you can start with situational awareness and then transition from that into the targeting aspect,” he said. “We’re not replacing anything and we’re not supplanting. It is genuinely enhancing and extending.”
Building the maritime awareness network
As previously mentioned, full situational awareness in the Pacific is more than just deploying assets and calling it a day. It is a network operation, and it carries with it the challenges of maintaining and sustaining a network in a hostile region.
Each component of the network has its own needs. Crewed surface vessels and aircraft operate under fuel restraints, so having refueling access in the region is needed. Submarines can only operate for so long before needing to resurface and resupply, so they need a place to dock and replenish. USVs can help with these challenges, but create their own issues, such as potentially being captured and reverse-engineered by adversaries to give away closely guarded technology secrets.
“There’s going to have to be some kind of a balance, which again points to the question of data distribution across the network,” said Zaientz. “Maybe you’ve got a bunch of these units that are attritable, low classification or unclassified that are merely passive data collectors. Maybe there’s a small number that are part of the network that have a more exquisite capability that should have a different set of controls attached to them; those have to be managed. The key element here is how do you have the sensor network be self-healing and self-managing within the constraints of this very hostile territory?”
Beyond that challenge is the challenge of operating USVs. Each crewed ship, submarine and aircraft has a dedicated crew, but it is not practical to have a 1:1 ratio of operators to vessels. Scaling a sensing force requires mission-level supervision: operators set coverage objectives and operating constraints, handle exceptions, and retain authority over mission execution while autonomy software coordinates routine tasks across vessels. When communications degrade, vessels must operate within approved mission parameters, coordinate locally where links remain available, and prioritize reporting as connectivity permits.
USVs can help establish what is expected in a certain area and then identify deviations from that pattern for further investigation or even potential engagement. For example, if boats are going through littoral areas in a certain pattern, they are likely following predetermined routes based on the depth of the water and maneuvering capabilities. If those patterns change or ships deviate from them, USVs can flag them so commanders can make a decision on what needs to be done, up to and including engaging hostile targets.
“You would want something that’s multi-mission so that you’ve got non-exquisite and exquisite USVs out there with those payloads,” said Pinx. “And if you see a deviation in the adversary’s pattern of life, you’re able to adjust for that in a way that a soldier, sailor, airman or Marine doesn’t necessarily have to put a lot of brain power behind it because the boats are adjusting in stride based off the rules of engagement or the mission parameters.”
Collaboration and cooperation
Building an infrastructure for true maritime awareness requires not only cooperation between branches of the US military, but also between the Pentagon and industry. By implementing consistent standards, modular architecture and clear requirements for capabilities, interoperability can be built into platforms from the start, instead of requiring troops in the field – or at sea – to figure out how to make systems work by cobbling together solutions or paging through technical manuals, said Pinx.
Lyntris’ work spans autonomous maritime platforms, mission-level autonomy and maritime command-and-control integration, giving the company a practical view of the challenges involved in bringing those capabilities together.
“The burden needs to be pulled up from servicemembers and put on the companies,” he said. “The government teams that are responsible for the acquisition and the requirements need to bake that in early and upfront so that by the time it gets down range, it is truly plug and play.”
There are efforts underway to make interoperability consistently available from the start, including open standards, modular open systems architecture and reference architectures from the government that help companies understand exactly what is needed and how it should be built to operate within the larger ecosystem. Standardized interfaces can reduce bespoke integration work and vendor lock-in, allowing proprietary technologies from different companies to operate within a shared architecture. That can make it easier to introduce new capabilities and replace or upgrade individual components.
“Historically, integration was point-to-point between vendors, lots of vendor lock,” said Zaientz. “The business models are based around vendor lock. The Air Force and the Navy who are collaborating on the autonomy government reference architecture – which is intended for air autonomy, but it’s starting to get visibility in the service community – are showing that if you have a consortium-based model, you get everyone together to work out a vendor-neutral set of mission threads and APIs, you can move really fast.”

articles.title: Cybercrime crackdown across Africa leads to 1,462 arrests, $105 million seized
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: More than 1,400 suspected cybercriminals were arrested across Africa this summer as part of a crackdown on the gangs perpetrating online fraud, ransomware and business email compromise attacks, Interpol said.
articles.full_text:
Cybercrime crackdown across Africa leads to 1,462 arrests, $105 million seized
More than 1,400 suspected cybercriminals were arrested across Africa this summer as part of an annual crackdown on the gangs perpetrating online fraud, ransomware and business email compromise (BEC) attacks, Interpol announced Thursday.
The law enforcement operation, dubbed Serengeti III, was said to have disrupted more than 10,000 malicious computer networks and recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds.
Just under 66,000 victims were identified, with cumulative losses exceeding $385 million. Previous operations in 2024 and 2025 tackled gangs also associated with millions in global losses.
Twenty African countries took part in the operation, alongside the United States, with Interpol providing investigators with intelligence regarding suspicious domains, IP addresses and command-and-control servers that were tied to criminal activity.
The largest number of arrests Interpol detailed came in Uganda, where law enforcement was described as dismantling two transnational fraud rings and arresting 365 foreign nationals.
Local media described some arrests in the country of individuals "mainly originating from Asia," although no specific nationalities were given. It is unclear whether those arrests were part of the same operation.
Another report, describing arrests in April, said more than 200 illegal immigrants were arrested alongside "a significant cache of computers of all types and IT equipment used to facilitate illegal gaming, betting and organized scamming."
Simon Mundeyi, a spokesman for the Ugandan Ministry of Internal Affairs, said the majority were from South and East Asia and were operating from an apartment complex that appeared to restrict their ability to exit.
Interpol said the groups in Uganda ran call centers that used scripts, fake trading platforms and fraudulent websites to persuade pensioners in Asia to put money into fictional investments.
In Angola, investigators shut down two illegal cryptocurrency mining centers, arresting nine people and seizing more than 2,000 mining devices. Police also confiscated six illegal power transformation stations, which Interpol valued at more than $1 million on their own.
It follows authorities in Angola raiding 25 mining centers allegedly operated by 60 Chinese nationals in Sergenti II last year.
In Nigeria, authorities arrested a suspect accused of running a phishing and BEC operation that harvested software credentials and amassed about 2.1 million email addresses. Investigators also seized a luxury car allegedly bought with the proceeds.
A separate Nigerian case, involving an investment scam promoted through messaging apps, led to one arrest and traced more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of it laundered through cryptocurrency.
Elsewhere, authorities took down a malicious mobile loan app scheme in Tanzania, disrupted a vehicle import fraud network operating on social media in Gabon, and arrested 30 people linked to a cybercrime operation in the Republic of Congo.
It follows police in Ghana and Nigeria arresting or detaining 28 people, and identifying more than 100 suspected victims of human trafficking, during a separate international operation targeting scam compounds in West Africa.
Interpol said several investigations remain open as authorities work to identify more suspects, trace illicit proceeds and analyze seized evidence.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

South Carolina officials offer assistance after state capital hit with cyberattack
The city of Columbia, South Carolina said it is responding to a cyberattack that has shut down several government systems.
A spokesperson told Recorded Future News that the city’s IT department recently identified suspicious activity and contacted the state’s South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED), which is now leading the investigation.
The systems impacted by the attack include the MyColaSC platform that citizens use to pay utility bills, report non-emergency issues and access other city services. The attack also knocked out Geographic Information Systems and systems underpinning animal services.
They urged residents to call to report concerns like potholes, fallen trees and broken streetlights while the MyColaSC platform was down.
Columbia is the capital city of South Carolina and has about 150,000 residents.
The city did not respond to questions about whether it is dealing with a ransomware attack. No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Wednesday.
“The City of Columbia wants to reassure residents that critical public safety and utility systems remain operational. These include the Columbia Police Department, Columbia-Richland Fire Department, 911 communications, Columbia Water systems and the Payment Center, including online payment services,” a city official said.
SLED declined to comment on the incident and directed all questions to Columbia officials.
The state previously dealt with a ransomware attack on the county of Spartanburg and a recent incident shut down the systems of large non-profit hospital system AnMed.
Columbia is one of the largest municipalities to face attacks in recent weeks as several smaller counties, cities and towns face off against criminal hackers. Cities and counties in Maryland, New Mexico, Utah, Texas, Nebraska, Missouri, Alaska, and Arizona have all dealt with service outages over the last three weeks due to cyberattacks and ransomware incidents.

articles.title: Meta on the spot for $25 billion under New Mexico privacy ruling
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal from a decade ago is still weighing on Meta's finances.
articles.full_text:
Meta on the spot for $25 billion under New Mexico privacy ruling
Meta must pay $25 billion in fines for data privacy violations related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal that became public almost 10 years ago, according to a New Mexico court filing released Wednesday.
In September, a jury found Meta had broken the state’s unfair practices law 43 million times for its role in the incident, which a whistleblower made public in 2018. Each violation carried civil penalties of as much as $5,000.
The state was initially awarded $220 billion, but state District Court Judge Francis Mathew reduced the penalty to $25 billion, according to the court filing. Meta will be charged 15% annual interest on the amount until the fine is paid off.
The case is tied to Meta-owned Facebook, which shared as many as 87 million users’ data with the Cambridge Analytica. The British political consulting firm then used the data to create psychological profiles of voters to facilitate targeted advertising, including in the 2016 presidential election.
New Mexico’s litigation focused on what Facebook told consumers about its data practices and how it combats misinformation and hate speech in the wake of the scandal becoming public, according to a press release from the office of Attorney General Raúl Torrez.
“The scale, duration, repetition, breadth, and willfulness of the violations, together with the evidence concerning Facebook's internal knowledge and practices … constitute substantial aggravating circumstances,” Mathew wrote in the filing.
Mathew highlighted the fact that senior Facebook leadership, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg and then-COO Sheryl Sandberg, created a calculated strategy to mislead consumers by among other things overseeing the creation of materials they called a “song sheet” to coordinate a public relations response.
“Facebook continued making public representations concerning users' control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement after employees, researchers, and senior personnel had internally identified that Facebook could not make good on its public promises,” the filing said, noting that Zuckerberg was aware of the deception.
The platform knew at the time that information regarding its data access infrastructure and enforcement protocols were not verifiable by users and the company took advantage of that, the filing said.
Facebook also failed to follow through on the “comprehensive” probe it promised consumers after the scandal became public, Mathew said.
The social media company was “aware at the time it made the promises that it did not have the ability to conduct such a thorough investigation or enforce deletion of the data due in large part to Facebook's poor record keeping and failure to vet third party developers at the time they were granted access to user data,” the filing said.
Pressure from senior leadership to minimize costs, a weak enforcement mechanism, poor investigative techniques and a focus on not setting a precedent for future probes caused Facebook to use an App Developer Investigation that was “willfully ineffective,” according to Mathew.
The ruling and Torrez’s approach to the enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
Meta plans to appeal the ruling, the statement said.
Torrez won $375 million in damages from Meta in March after a jury found the tech behemoth broke state law related to its kids’online safety practices.
Meta has already faced steep fines related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, including a $459 million penalty that was included in a roughly $17 billion August settlement with a group of several other state attorneys general pursuing the tech giant for its child safety practices.
The social media company also settled a class action lawsuit related to the scandal in 2022 for $725 million.
Digital freedoms advocates hailed the momentum states are gaining as they target Meta and other big tech companies for violating users’ data privacy.
"The message from these state actions is evident: companies must be accurate and clear about how they process and treat data,” Eric Null, director of the Privacy and Data Project at the Center for Democracy and Technology, said via email.
“If companies don’t improve their practices, states should ratchet up the pressure by continuing to hold companies accountable under current law and updating their privacy statutes to prevent such harms from happening in the first place."
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Tech trio launches $10 million initiative to help under-resourced utilities bolster cybersecurity
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Up to 500 under-resourced utilities will receive support in order to bolster their cybersecurity through a private sector initiative launched this week.
articles.full_text:
Tech trio launches $10 million initiative to help under-resourced utilities bolster cybersecurity
Up to 500 under-resourced utilities will get access to a range of free cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and training through a new program offered by the global services company Accenture, the cybersecurity firm Dragos and the SANS Institute training organization.
The three organizations announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation on Tuesday, offering to provide eligible utilities with operational technology-focused cybersecurity services and more. They are collectively investing $10 million into the foundation.
The program is available to any U.S.-based water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue — which the companies said accounts for 97% of utilities.
Participants will get access to cybersecurity tools from Dragos, which notifies organizations of the devices on their network and ways they can address vulnerabilities.
Accenture will assist with deploying the tools and configuring them for participants. The company will also provide ongoing support for the utilities as they integrate the tools into their operations.
The SANS Institute will offer training to help build utilities’ employees capacity.
The initiative follows breaches of more than 100 water utilities across the U.S.. Government agencies continue to warn of both Chinese and Russian cyberattacks on energy utilties, telecoms and more.
Dragos CEO Robert Lee said cybercriminals and nation-states are “aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans.”
The foundation “gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost,” he added.
Members of the program will also have access to one another, allowing them to share best practices and operational experience.
“The best security technology in the world won’t protect a utility if its staff are not able to use it. The foundation puts training and skills in the hands of the people protecting the water, power, natural gas, and wastewater treatment systems that communities rely on,” said James Lyne, CEO of the SANS Institute.
The first phase of the program will involve 500 utilities and may expand depending on its success.
Cyber defenders have for years warned the public that most of the utilities in the U.S. cannot afford the cybersecurity tools needed to protect themselves against an array of evolving threats that include ransomware gangs, nation-state actors and other cybercriminals eager to cause damage.
Many utilities lack the funding, staffing and technological capacity to integrate cybersecurity tools — leaving thousands of pumps, valves, substations, and distribution networks vulnerable to attack.
There is no federal or state government involvement in the program. The cybersecurity company Elastic will also offer technical support to help scale the program.
There is no time limit on how long participants will have access to the program and Dragos said “other companies are already expressing interest in coming on board to grow it further.”
After the attacks on water utilities in July, the National Rural Water Association (NRWA) launched its own program involving five managed detection and response providers — Rapid7, Defendify, Legato Security, L1 Secure and Sentinel Technologies — who agreed to share threat information and data on vulnerability patches.
Federal efforts to improve the cybersecurity of utilities have stagnated, leaving states to create their own frameworks for protecting water, power, telecoms and more.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.
